    13  /-!
    14  # Comparing sums and integrals
    15  
    16  ## Summary
    17  
    18  It is often the case that error terms in analysis can be computed by comparing
    19  an infinite sum to the improper integral of an antitone function.
    20  
    21  It contains several lemmas in this direction, for antitone or monotone functions
    22  (or products of antitone and monotone functions), formulated for sums on `range i` or `Ico a b`.
    23  These are used to prove a version of the integral test for antitone functions.
    24  
    25  ## Main Results
    26  
    27  * `AntitoneOn.integral_le_sum`: The integral of an antitone function is at most the sum of its
    28    values at integer steps aligning with the left-hand side of the interval.
    29  * `AntitoneOn.sum_le_integral`: The sum of an antitone function along integer steps aligning with
    30    the right-hand side of the interval is at most the integral of the function along that interval
    31  * `MonotoneOn.integral_le_sum`: The integral of a monotone function is at most the sum of its
    32    values at integer steps aligning with the right-hand side of the interval.
    33  * `MonotoneOn.sum_le_integral`: The sum of a monotone function along integer steps aligning with
    34    the left-hand side of the interval is at most the integral of the function along that interval
    35  * `sum_mul_Ico_le_integral_of_monotone_antitone`: the sum of `f i * g i` on an interval is bounded
    36    by the integral of `f x * g (x - 1)` if `f` is monotone and `g` is antitone.
    37  * `integral_le_sum_mul_Ico_of_antitone_monotone`: the sum of `f i * g i` on an interval is bounded
    38    below by the integral of `f x * g (x - 1)` if `f` is antitone and `g` is monotone.
    39  * `AntitoneOn.summable_of_integrableOn_Ioi_zero` and `AntitoneOn.tsum_le_integral`, the
    40    integral test for antitone functions.
"}]

    17  In this file we prove some properties of `∫ x in s, f x ∂μ`. Recall that this notation
    18  is defined as `∫ x, f x ∂(μ.restrict s)`. In `integral_indicator` we prove that for a measurable
    19  function `f` and a measurable set `s` this definition coincides with another natural definition:
    20  `∫ x, indicator s f x ∂μ = ∫ x in s, f x ∂μ`, where `indicator s f x` is equal to `f x` for `x ∈ s`
    21  and is zero otherwise.
    22  
    23  Since `∫ x in s, f x ∂μ` is a notation, one can rewrite or apply any theorem about `∫ x, f x ∂μ`
    24  directly. In this file we prove some theorems about dependence of `∫ x in s, f x ∂μ` on `s`, e.g.
    25  `setIntegral_union`, `setIntegral_empty`, `setIntegral_univ`.

    31  
    32  ## Notation
